rv.q: I am relieved—even a little surprised—to report that the show, which opened last night at the Henry Miller, still manages to be both escapist and nasty fun, frivolous yet pertinent, and fills a bit of the darkness with elevated foolishness of a very high order.
Yet it is still the same superb production with a terrific cast and an adventurous score that sounds better the second time around.
The ultimate fringe success continues to delight audiences even though, after three years, some of the original cast members have inevitably moved on.

This show is a carefully balanced and very well-directed high wire act that keeps several balls spinning and twirling in the air simultaneously, thanks to the facility of director John Rando and the genius of John Carrafa, who has staged the musical numbers.
Recent memory provides no comparable example of a musical with an equally dazzling and talented cast.
But when you come down to it, a musical about the right to pee freely is basically just dumb.
It's alive and well and living in Urinetown—the show that gives New York a chance to laugh and to heal at the same time.
Those of us who love musicals will (you should pardon the expression) lap Urinetown up.

aw.sub: Won Best Book of a Musical + 2 more

cn.t: This wacky musical satire about pay toilets wins over most critics with its witty, irreverent humor and adventurous score, though a few find the parody doesn't quite hold water.

vs.sum: A Roundabout Theatre Company house with excellent sightlines and good sound. Post-renovation seating is comfortable with decent legroom. Standout facilities include 30 women's restroom stalls — triple the building code requirement — virtually eliminating intermission lines.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. 3 hearing loops. 100 Sennheiser hearing devices. 12 wheelchair seats.
